clue.text: Take off clothing quietly — like sex naked and calm

indicators.note: To clothe a thing is to put a covering right round it, so the word in front closes over the letter named next.

parts.note: to take somebody off is to ape them, copying their voice and manner
p is the musician's mark for piano, meaning play it softly
'as' does the job of 'like' in a comparison: quick as a flash

indicators.note: Something naked has had its outer covering stripped off, so the word loses the letters at both ends and only its middle survives.

parts.note: take the letters off either end of the word and its middle letter is what is left

explanation.surface: Clothes coming off quietly, and sex spoken of as bare and unhurried.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off clothing' reads as one act of undressing, and the split really falls after 'Take off', where the sense wanted is imitate.
explanation.definitionFit: To appease is to calm somebody down by giving them what they want, so 'calm' is the verb it stands in for.

clue.text: Can holding on then playing, win?

indicators.note: Holding something means keeping it inside you, so the word in front shuts round the letters named after it.

parts.note: a pail is a can in the bucket sense, the thing you carry water in
re means on the subject of, the way a memo heading is written
v is versus in a fixture list, the two sides playing each other

explanation.surface: Someone gripping on, then getting into the game — can they win?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like the modal verb opening a question, matching the question mark at the end, and it is a plain noun for a bucket.
explanation.definitionFit: To prevail is to win out — the sense in 'good sense prevailed', where one side comes through a contest on top.

clue.text: Prepare ecstasy and crack

parts.note: e is the tablet, ecstasy, in the crossword's drug shorthand
a crack is a wisecrack, a quick joke at somebody's expense

explanation.surface: Somebody laying out drugs, ecstasy and crack, before a night out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' is dragged into the drugs picture by the ecstasy sitting beside it, and the sense wanted is the one you make at a party.
explanation.definitionFit: To equip is to prepare somebody by supplying what they need: 'prepare for battle' and 'equip for battle' ask for the same thing.

clue.text: One questioning pussy stopped by opening of catflap

indicators.note: To stop a gap is to plug it, so the letter named next is pushed into the middle of the word before.

parts.note: a wound gone pussy is full of pus, which is what septic means

parts.note: the first letter of 'catflap'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pussy' is planted to be read as the cat the catflap belongs to, and the word it wants is the medical adjective about pus.
explanation.definitionFit: A sceptic is somebody who questions what they are told instead of accepting it, so 'One questioning' names them by that habit.

clue.text: England through winning match

indicators.note: 'Winning' is doing loose duty as a taking-in instruction: what you win you take, and here one word takes the other inside it.

parts.note: you go by the back road, meaning through it
a match is a light — 'have you got a light?' asks for one

explanation.surface: England coming through a win in a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' looks like the fixture the win belongs to and is the thing you strike. Soldiers brought the word home from India, where bilayati meant foreign.
explanation.definitionFit: Blighty is the soldier's fond name for home, so it means Britain in general and 'England' points at it loosely rather than exactly.

clue.text: Contact newspaper: passage having line moved to top

indicators.note: In a down entry the top is the first square, so the letter named is lifted out of where it sits and rewritten at the front.

parts.note: l is the standard short form of line, as in a printed line of text
the i is a British daily paper whose whole name is one letter
an aisle is the passage between rows of seats, and it hands its l away to the front

explanation.surface: An editor ringing a newspaper to have a line of copy moved to the top of a passage.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes 'newspaper: passage' look like a paper and its column, when the two words are separate pieces of the build.
explanation.definitionFit: To liaise is to be in contact: the officer who liaises keeps two groups talking, which is 'Contact' used as a verb.

clue.text: Enraged drunk covering up wearing syrup

indicators.note: A drunk cannot walk a straight line, and the letters he is carrying come out in no reliable order.
Covering something up hides it, so the letters named next end up buried inside the shuffled ones.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
if you are wearing a coat you are in it

explanation.surface: A furious drunk hiding himself under a wig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Syrup' is Cockney rhyming slang for a wig — syrup of figs — which is the picture the surface paints, while the definition wants the bottled sweetener.
explanation.definitionFit: Grenadine is the deep red pomegranate syrup poured into cocktails, so 'syrup' names it by exactly what it is.

clue.text: Protecting a turtle at sea

indicators.note: A turtle at sea is adrift with nothing holding it in place, and the letters beside the phrase drift the same way.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: Conservationists guarding a turtle out in the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: Tutelar is the rare adjective behind 'tutelary deity', the guardian who watches over a place, and 'at sea' finishes the turtle picture while doing the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutelar means acting as a guardian, so 'Protecting' is the same idea: a tutelar saint is the one protecting a town.

clue.text: Flooring Keir Starmer — depict end, primarily lost to Reform

indicators.note: What is lost is the primary letter, the one at the very front of the little word beside it, dropped before anything else happens.
Reform is re-forming: the letters are made up again into a different shape, and the party's name is doing that job in disguise.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seventeen letters
END gives up the letter at its front, and the two left join the fodder

explanation.surface: Keir Starmer floored, his image undone as support drains away to Reform.
explanation.walkthrough: Kidderminster is a Worcestershire town that ran the British carpet trade, so its name became a kind of carpet; 'Reform' reads as the party and is the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A Kidderminster carpet is a flat reversible weave with no pile, and a carpet is flooring — the definition names the class it belongs to.

clue.text: Land every uppercut in left side

parts.note: per means for each: sixty miles per hour is sixty for every hour

indicators.note: Reading across, a word's left side is the end it starts at, so only the letter sitting there is taken.

parts.note: the left-hand end of the word is its first letter, and that is all that is wanted

explanation.surface: Landing an uppercut on somebody's left side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Land' opens the clue as the verb a punch does, and it is the definition — the boxing match is surface only, right down to the uppercut being a word rather than a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: Peru is a country, so 'Land' defines it by class: one word naming what sort of thing the answer is.

clue.text: I get erect when excited hugging adult that might be hot in drag?

definitions.text: that might be hot in drag?

indicators.note: Somebody excited will not keep still, and neither do the letters standing in front of the phrase.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
a was the cinema certificate for an adult audience

explanation.surface: A frank boast about getting aroused while hugging an adult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In drag' points at a drag queen in the surface, and the heat is real: a drag is the pull you take on the thing.
explanation.definitionFit: You take a drag on an e-cigarette and its coil heats up, so 'hot in drag' describes what it does whenever it is used.

clue.text: See 9 Down
Home-improvement work with little drilling, sadly

indicators.note: A drill bores into a thing and leaves a hole, and that hole is where the word beside it is dropped in.

parts.note: do-it-yourself, the three letters every British hardware shop trades on
little and small are the same word for size

explanation.surface: A home-improvement job done with barely any drilling, and it shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With little drilling' reads as a complaint about a botched job, and 'sadly' at the end looks like the setter's sigh rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dismally means in a dreary, low-spirited way, so it stands in for 'sadly' in the sense of failing badly: the job went dismally.

clue.text: Lay down part of hand — one folded at table?

parts.note: to place something is to lay it down where you want it
a hand at cards is made of them, one card at a time

explanation.surface: A poker player laying down part of a hand and folding at the table.
explanation.walkthrough: Folding at the table is the poker move the surface sells, and the answer folds literally: a stiff little card standing at each setting.
explanation.definitionFit: A place card is the folded card printed with a guest's name and stood at their seat, which is what 'one folded at table' describes.

clue.text: Attention-seeker online to get on with bachelor needing sex

parts.note: two people who click get on with each other from the start
a bachelor's degree, the graduate's two letters
'it' has meant sex appeal since the 1920s, when Clara Bow was the It girl

explanation.surface: A lonely bachelor online, chasing attention and after sex.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as a personal ad, and 'online' is the word that pins the definition to a modern noun rather than to a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Clickbait is a headline written to make you click rather than to inform you, so it seeks attention online exactly as the definition says.

clue.text: Supporter following most of top stars

definitions.note: 'Stars' is plural where the answer is one sign, which is fair twice over: a constellation is a group of stars, and a newspaper's stars are the zodiac taken as a set.

indicators.note: Most of a word is not all of it: keep everything except the letter it ends on.
What follows comes after, so the supporter's letters are written second, behind the ones already taken.

parts.note: a lid is the top of a jar, with its last letter dropped
the undergarment that supports, and a crossword regular

explanation.surface: A fan who follows most of the top stars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top stars' reads as celebrities, and the two words belong to opposite halves of the clue: one is a jar lid, the other the zodiac.
explanation.definitionFit: Libra is one of the twelve zodiac signs, the constellation of the scales, so 'stars' points at it as one of the horoscope's set.

clue.text: Holiday resort surrounded by country

parts.note: a spa is a resort built round mineral springs, Bath or Baden-Baden
whatever you are surrounded by, you are in

explanation.surface: A holiday resort with open countryside all round it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surrounded by' looks like the instruction to put one piece inside another, and it is a two-letter word in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain is a country, so the definition names the class the answer belongs to and asks for nothing cleverer.

clue.text: Item of crockery placed on gold table

indicators.note: In a down entry, whatever is placed on a thing sits above it, so the first piece is written before the second.

parts.note: the flat round thing your dinner arrives on
au is gold's symbol on the periodic table, from the Latin aurum

explanation.surface: A plate set down on a gold table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gold table' reads as one piece of expensive furniture, and the two words split: the first is a chemical symbol, the second the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plateau is a tableland, a raised flat stretch of country, and 'table' is the geographer's own word for that shape.

clue.text: Older children learn about English name

indicators.note: Turning about is facing the other way, so the word in front of it is written back to front.

parts.note: your big brother is your older one
ch is the standard short form for children

e for English, as on a language label

explanation.surface: Older children learning about an English name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Older children learn' reads as one classroom scene and every word of it is a separate piece; the definition is the single word left at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A big cheese is the important person in an organisation — a big name — so 'name' works in the sense of somebody who matters.

clue.text: Horse and cocaine runs through old addict

indicators.note: Something running through a thing passes into its middle, so the letter named goes inside the words beside it.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse' is heroin in the surface's drug picture and an actual animal in the definition: a courser is the poet's word for a swift mount.
explanation.definitionFit: A courser is a swift horse, the charger a knight rode into battle, a word now kept alive mostly by poetry and crosswords.

clue.text: Relaxed and went out after a lot of sex

indicators.note: A lot of a word is most but not all of it, so the letter it ends on is left behind.
What comes after is written second, so the longer piece follows the two letters taken in front of it.

parts.note: the word for sex with its last letter dropped
to date somebody is to go out with them

explanation.surface: Somebody perfectly calm after a night out and plenty of sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relaxed and went out' reads as one description of an easy evening, and the definition stops dead after the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedated means calmed by a drug, so 'Relaxed' fits it as a state somebody has been put into rather than one they chose.

clue.text: Folds money

definitions.meaning: a fold is a pen for sheep, and the municipal version is where stray animals were shut in

explanation.surface: Somebody folding banknotes.
explanation.walkthrough: Two nouns and nothing else, so the clue offers no seam to find. The animal-pen sense is the older one, still alive in 'the dog pound'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pound is the enclosure stray animals were shut into, the job a fold does for sheep; and pounds are Britain's money.

clue.text: Bowls over grass to get prizes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' is the green the bowls roll over in the surface, and the smokeable kind in the wordplay.

clue.text: Winning team getting advantage

parts.note: a team two goals up is winning by two

explanation.definitionFit: The upside of a situation is the good that can come out of it, so 'advantage' is the benefit you are left holding.

clue.text: Rogue to con prince

parts.note: a con and a scam are the same swindle

explanation.definitionFit: A scamp is a rogue of the mild sort, a mischief-maker and usually a child, rather than anybody genuinely criminal.

clue.text: Unsold books and souvenirs outside front of airport

indicators.note: What stands outside goes round the outside of what follows, one word closing over the letter named next.

parts.note: a souvenir is a keepsake, something that reminds you of a place

parts.note: the first letter of 'airport'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Books and souvenirs' reads as one gift-shop window, and the definition stops after the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: Remainders are the unsold copies a publisher clears cheaply on the trade, so 'Unsold books' is the bookseller's own term for them.

clue.text: Book performers

the turns on a variety bill, each one a slot in the running order

explanation.definitionFit: Acts of the Apostles is a book of the New Testament, and acts are the performers on a variety bill: two everyday senses of one short word.

clue.text: Extremely short experiment on rat

parts.note: a rat and a cur are both names for a contemptible person
a test is an experiment, the laboratory kind

clue.text: School gripped by teacher retiring after last of one-night stands

indicators.note: To be gripped by something is to be held tight inside it, so the piece named first goes within the word that follows.
The last of a word is the letter it ends on, and that one letter is all that is taken.
A teacher retiring is on the way out, and those letters go out the way they came in: written back to front.

parts.note: the final letter of 'one-night'

a school of whales goes by another name, and it is three letters long

explanation.definitionFit: A tripod is the three-legged stand that holds a camera or a telescope steady, so 'stands' names them by the job they do.
